design_detail: Multi-part laboratory report with a small human analytical series and three animal experiments. (1) Human samples, described but not appraised here as a design: cocaethylene concentrations measured in post-mortem blood from 7 people who had used both cocaine and ethanol, whose samples were sent to the authors by a county medical examiner's laboratory because chromatographic peaks presumptively identified as cocaethylene had been seen; and in blood from emergency-department patients selected on the basis of urine benzoylecgonine and blood alcohol results. Incubation experiments tested whether cocaethylene could form in a sample after collection. (2) Rat tissue: inhibition of [3H]dopamine uptake into synaptosomes and of [3H]GBR 12935 binding to striatal membranes, cocaine against cocaethylene. (3) Rats in vivo: extracellular dopamine in the nucleus accumbens by microdialysis after intravenous cocaine, cocaethylene or saline; and locomotor activity and rearing over 15 minutes after intraperitoneal cocaine, cocaethylene or saline, scored by one observer blind to treatment, with random assignment to the three groups. (4) Three rhesus monkeys trained to self-administer intravenous cocaine on a fixed-ratio 30 schedule, with cocaethylene substituted across a dose range. Nothing was given to people in this study.
can_establish: That cocaethylene was present, sometimes at concentrations above those of cocaine, in post-mortem and emergency-department blood from people who had used cocaine and ethanol together, and was essentially absent when ethanol was not; that it did not form in blood or acid after collection under the conditions tested; and that in rats and monkeys cocaethylene acted on the dopamine uptake system and maintained self-administration much as cocaine did.
cannot_establish: That cocaethylene caused or contributed to any death (the 7 post-mortem cases are a selected series with no cause of death, no comparison group and no denominator); that cocaethylene produces cocaine-like effects in people, or how potent it is in people; the relative toxicity of cocaethylene and cocaine in any species (no toxicity outcome was measured here); or what the combination of cocaine, ethanol and cocaethylene together does, which the authors state their experiments did not address.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable to the animal work. The human samples were not recruited: post-mortem samples came from a county medical examiner's laboratory, which sent them because peaks presumptively identified as cocaethylene had already been seen in them; the hospital samples were picked out from emergency-department specimens on the basis of urine benzoylecgonine and blood alcohol results (pp. 1787–1788).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Human samples: selected by prior analytical findings as above; no clinical criteria, no cause or manner of death and no demographic information are given. Animals: no inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: None reported for the 7 people whose blood was analysed (no age, sex, cause of death or circumstances). Rat strain, sex, weight and supplier are not reported; monkey sex and weight are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: The 7 post-mortem samples are a doubly selected series: they reached the laboratory because a chromatographic peak suggesting cocaethylene had already been seen, so they cannot show how often cocaethylene is present among deaths, and no comparison deaths were analysed. The hospital samples were chosen by their benzoylecgonine and alcohol results, which makes the comparison between ethanol-positive and ethanol-negative samples informative about whether cocaethylene tracks ethanol, but not about prevalence. The animal experiments used small groups with unequal numbers (4 against 7 in the microdialysis comparison).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine and cocaethylene by reversed-phase ion-pairing high-performance liquid chromatography, with identity confirmed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (molecular ion at m/e 317 and ions at m/e 196 and 212 for cocaethylene, against m/e 303, 182 and 198 for cocaine); cocaethylene standard synthesized in the authors' laboratory, 97–99% pure and free of cocaine. Blood ethanol by the referring laboratories' own methods, reported in mg/dl (pp. 1788–1789). In the animal work the drugs were given by the investigators.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, all in animals: rats, cocaine or cocaethylene 1 mg/kg intravenously for microdialysis, and 10 mg/kg intraperitoneally 5 minutes before a 15-minute behavioural test; rhesus monkeys, intravenous injections contingent on 30 lever presses with a 45-second timeout, in four 25-minute components separated by 10-minute periods without drug, over a standard cocaine dose range of 0.001 to 0.03 mg/kg per injection, with cocaethylene substituted over 0.001 to 0.03 mg/kg per injection in two monkeys and 0.003 to 0.1 mg/kg per injection in a third (pp. 1788–1789).
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the human part: cocaethylene was looked for only in samples that also contained cocaine or benzoylecgonine, and its presence is reported against blood ethanol. Post-mortem ethanol ranged from 20 to 240 mg/dl, and other drugs in those 7 people are not reported. The animals received one compound at a time.

comparison.controls: Animal work: saline-injected rats for microdialysis and behaviour; within-assay comparison of cocaethylene against cocaine for uptake and binding; each monkey's own cocaine dose-response curve from the sessions immediately before cocaethylene substitution. Human work: samples positive for cocaine but negative for ethanol (n = 14) serve as a comparison for whether cocaethylene appears without ethanol; there is no comparison group of deaths.
comparison.matching: None described; rats were randomly assigned to saline, cocaine or cocaethylene for the behavioural test (p. 1788).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the animal experiments. For the 7 people, nothing is known before death: no health information, no drug-use history, no amount or timing of use, and no cause or manner of death.

outcomes.instruments: Blood concentrations of cocaethylene and cocaine (HPLC, GC-MS). Inhibition of [3H]dopamine uptake into rat synaptosomes and of [3H]GBR 12935 binding to rat striatal membranes, as concentration-response curves. Extracellular dopamine in the nucleus accumbens by microdialysis with electrochemical detection (detection limit 2–3 fmol injected), expressed as a percentage of the pre-injection level. Locomotor activity counted as crossings of quadrant markings and rearing as lifting both forepaws off the ground, over 15 minutes, by one observer blind to treatment. Rate of lever responding (responses per second) in monkeys (pp. 1788–1789).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assay identity was confirmed by mass spectrometry and the synthesized standard was characterized; no assay precision, recovery or limit of quantitation is reported for the blood measurements, and no post-mortem specimen site, interval since death or storage conditions are given for the 7 cases.
outcomes.operationalization: Nothing is operationalized as harm, toxicity or cause of death. 'Reinforcing' is operationalized as maintaining lever responding in monkeys; 'activation' as quadrant crossings and rears in rats.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None described beyond the stated analysis: ANOVA followed where appropriate by the Newman-Keuls test, with P < 0.05 as the level of significance (p. 1789).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Behavioural ratings were made by one observer blind to treatment (p. 1788). Blinding is not mentioned for the microdialysis, assay or monkey work; those outcomes are instrument-recorded.

analysis.effect_sizes: Concentrations and percentages, with no confidence intervals and no test statistics printed anywhere in the paper. Post-mortem cocaethylene 73 to 1447 ng/ml against cocaine 34 to 4370 ng/ml and ethanol 20 to 240 mg/dl in the same 7 samples (Table I, p. 1789); cocaethylene exceeded cocaine in 4 of the 7 (editors' calculation from Table I: ratios 0.33, 1.30, 1.21, 0.78, 0.39, 2.15 and 1.56). Inhibition of [3H]GBR 12935 binding, IC50 300 nM, and of [3H]dopamine uptake, IC50 250 nM, with no significant difference between cocaethylene and cocaine (pp. 1789–1790). Microdialysis: about a four-fold rise in accumbens dopamine after cocaethylene 1 mg/kg, not significantly different from cocaine at the same dose; mean baseline dopamine corrected for probe recovery 10.4 ± 2.1 fmol/microlitre (p. 1790, Fig. 3). Monkeys: the mean maximum rate-maintaining dose was 0.01 mg/kg per injection for cocaethylene against 0.03 mg/kg per injection for cocaine (p. 1792).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration; none would be expected for this design and period. No animal-care or ethics approval statement appears in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only group means are shown for the rat experiments, as figures; no numerical table, no standard deviations and no test statistics are given. Separate IC50 values for cocaine and for cocaethylene are not printed, so the claim that they are equipotent cannot be checked against two numbers.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 4 to 7 rats per group and 3 monkeys, the repeated statements that cocaethylene and cocaine did not differ are non-significant results in very small samples and do not establish equivalence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Cocaethylene was present in blood from people who had used cocaine and ethanol together, at concentrations that in 4 of 7 post-mortem samples exceeded cocaine's, and was almost always absent when ethanol was not present; it did not form in the sample after collection under the conditions tested. In rat tissue and in rats and monkeys it behaved much like cocaine at the dopamine uptake system, in raising accumbens dopamine, in increasing locomotion and rearing, and in maintaining self-administration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary states that the formation of this active homolog of cocaine 'may contribute to the effects and consequences' of combined cocaine and ethanol use (p. 1787) and the Discussion that the concentrations found were comparable to, and often above, cocaine concentrations known to be pharmacologically active (p. 1792); both are offered as possibilities. The authors are explicit that the effects of the drugs in combination were not addressed by their experiments (p. 1793) and that cross-tolerance, sensitization and better brain penetration are speculation ('might'). The one place where wording outruns the data is the summary's statement that cocaethylene was approximately equipotent to cocaine in maintaining responding, where the Results give a mean maximum rate-maintaining dose three times lower for cocaethylene (0.01 against 0.03 mg/kg per injection) in 3 monkeys with visible individual variation. Nothing in the paper claims that cocaethylene caused the deaths, and the card's own caution is that the 7 cases establish presence only.

timeline.event: Hearn et al. (cited here as refs 4–6 and in the companion literature): cocaethylene has high affinity for the dopamine transporter
Bradberry et al. (cited here, ref 12 and later work): microdialysis comparison of brain cocaine and cocaethylene levels and their effects on dopamine and serotonin
Intravenous cocaethylene compared with cocaine in people with cocaine dependence: cocaine-like but less potent on heart rate and rated effects
Fractional conversion of intravenous cocaine to cocaethylene measured in people with labelled compounds: about 17% of the dose, with cocaethylene concentrations far below cocaine's

replication.where_it_stands: The analytical observation, that cocaethylene is formed when cocaine and alcohol are used together and can reach concentrations comparable with cocaine's, has held up and was later quantified in people under controlled dosing (Harris et al., 2003). The animal pharmacology has been extended rather than overturned. What this paper opened and did not answer, how much cocaethylene contributes to the effects or the dangers of combined use in people, is still open: the direct human comparison found cocaethylene less potent than cocaine (Hart et al., 2000), and in the controlled human study cocaethylene concentrations stayed well below cocaine's.

funding.funder: Grants DA 05119, DA 04050 and DA 04403 (National Institute on Drug Abuse grant numbers; the funding body is not named in the acknowledgement) (p. 1793).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the departments of laboratory medicine, psychiatry and pharmacology at one university medical school and the department of pharmacology at another. The acknowledgement states that the post-mortem samples for cocaethylene analysis and identification were provided by a named toxicologist at a county medical examiner's office (p. 1793); that laboratory had itself flagged the presumptive peaks, which is the selection route described above.

what_would_settle_it: For the human question: a consecutive series of deaths in which cocaine was found, with cocaethylene, ethanol and cocaine measured in a defined specimen at a recorded interval after death in every case, compared with deaths from other causes in the same population, so that presence can be given a denominator. For the pharmacological question: concentrations of cocaethylene in people reaching those measured in post-mortem blood, with cardiac and hepatic outcomes measured, which ethics would not permit directly and which therefore has to be approached through the natural experiment of combined use.

domains.note: Rats in the behavioural experiment were randomly assigned to saline, cocaine or cocaethylene (p. 1788), but the method is not described; for the microdialysis and tissue experiments no allocation is described, and the microdialysis groups are unequal (4, 7 and 7).
Rat strain, sex, weight range and supplier are not reported anywhere, and no baseline measures are given per group apart from a pooled mean baseline dopamine concentration.
Housing is not described; rats were habituated to the test boxes for three hours on two days before the behavioural test, but cage and chamber assignment is not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Not reported for the microdialysis or monkey work; for the behavioural test only the observer is described as blind, not the person injecting.
The order in which animals were tested or dialysed is not reported, and in the monkeys cocaethylene was always substituted after cocaine rather than in a randomized order.
The behavioural ratings, the one observer-dependent outcome, were made blind to treatment; dopamine, binding, uptake and lever responses were instrument-recorded.
No losses, exclusions or failed probe placements are reported for any experiment, and the unequal group sizes in the microdialysis experiment are not explained.

No protocol (none would be expected in 1991). Every experiment named in the Methods is reported, but only as figures with group means and no test statistics, and separate IC50 values for the two compounds are not printed.

No animal-care or ethics approval statement. In the monkeys, cocaethylene was substituted in animals already trained and maintained on cocaine, with the comparison drawn against the immediately preceding cocaine sessions, so order and history are confounded with the drug. The decimal points in the axis labels of the self-administration figure are not legible on the printed page, so the dose and response values can be read only from the text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE defines no overall judgment; this is the editors' summary, set to the most severe judgment among the items bearing on the main animal findings. The animal experiments are small, incompletely described (no strain, sex or weights, no ethics statement) and reported without test statistics, and the monkey comparison is confounded with order; the one blinded outcome is a strength. The human part of the paper is not an animal design and is not covered by SYRCLE: it is a selected analytical series of 7 post-mortem samples with no comparison deaths, no denominator and no cause of death, and the editors treat it as a case series whose only secure content is presence and concentration. Cite this source for the identification of cocaethylene in blood after combined cocaine and ethanol use, for the concentrations in those 7 samples, for its near-absence in samples without ethanol, for the incubation experiments ruling out formation after collection, and, labelled as rat and monkey findings, for cocaethylene acting at the dopamine uptake system and maintaining self-administration. Do not cite it for cocaethylene causing death or harm in people, for prevalence among deaths, or for potency in people.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rats (strain, sex, weight and supplier not reported) for synaptosome uptake, striatal membrane binding, nucleus accumbens microdialysis (cocaine n = 4, cocaethylene n = 7, saline n = 7) and behaviour (n = 5 per group); rhesus monkeys (n = 3, sex not reported) for self-administration.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Rats: cocaine or cocaethylene 1 mg/kg intravenously (microdialysis, with sampling from 40 minutes before to 80 minutes after injection) and 10 mg/kg intraperitoneally 5 minutes before a 15-minute behavioural test. Monkeys: intravenous injections on a fixed-ratio 30 schedule with a 45-second timeout, in four 25-minute components per session separated by 10-minute periods without drug; cocaine 0.001–0.03 mg/kg per injection as the standard range, cocaethylene substituted in single daily sessions over 0.001–0.03 mg/kg per injection in two monkeys and 0.003–0.1 mg/kg per injection in a third.
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given by the paper and none calculated here. The animal doses were chosen for the assays and schedules, not scaled to any human exposure, and the human blood concentrations reported in the same paper come from people whose doses are unknown.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Only in part. Intravenous self-administration in monkeys is a standard model of drug taking, but cocaethylene was given to animals as a pure compound, while in people it is formed inside the body from cocaine and alcohol and appears alongside both of them; the controlled human study of this question found cocaethylene concentrations far below cocaine's (Harris et al., 2003). Single injections in rats model neither repeated use nor the combination.

key_findings.finding: In post-mortem blood from 7 people who had used cocaine and ethanol, cocaethylene ranged from 73 to 1447 ng/ml alongside cocaine 34 to 4370 ng/ml and ethanol 20 to 240 mg/dl; cocaethylene exceeded cocaine in 4 of the 7 samples.
key_findings.note: Presence and concentration only: the paper gives no cause or manner of death, no specimen site, no interval since death and no comparison deaths, and the samples were sent precisely because cocaethylene peaks had been seen in them.

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene tracked ethanol in living patients: 10 of 17 emergency-department blood samples whose urine was positive for benzoylecgonine and whose blood contained ethanol showed cocaethylene, and 6 of the 7 cocaethylene-negative samples held either no cocaine or less than 5 ng/ml; of 14 further samples positive on cocaine screening but negative for ethanol, 13 showed no cocaethylene and one a trace.

Cocaethylene did not form in samples after collection in the conditions tested: no cocaethylene appeared when 400 ng/ml of cocaine and of benzoylecgonine were incubated in blood containing ethanol (500 mg/dl) at 37 °C for an hour and at refrigerator temperature for 24 days, or when 500 ng/ml of each was incubated with 4 g/dl alcohol in 0.1 M hydrochloric acid at 37 °C for two hours.

In rat tissue, cocaethylene and cocaine did not differ detectably at the dopamine uptake system: inhibition of [3H]GBR 12935 binding to striatal membranes with an IC50 of 300 nM, and inhibition of [3H]dopamine uptake into synaptosomes from striatum or nucleus accumbens with an IC50 of 250 nM.
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph (p. 1789) continuing on p. 1790; Fig. 2
key_findings.note: One IC50 is printed per assay, without separate values for the two compounds and without a test statistic, so 'no significant difference' cannot be checked numerically.

key_findings.finding: In rats, intravenous cocaethylene 1 mg/kg raised extracellular dopamine in the nucleus accumbens about four-fold above the pre-injection level at 20 minutes, not significantly different from cocaine at the same dose, while saline did not change it; mean baseline dopamine corrected for probe recovery was 10.4 ± 2.1 fmol per microlitre.
key_findings.note: Read from the figure at 300 dpi: both drug curves peak near 390–400% at 20 minutes and fall to about 140% (cocaethylene) and 100% (cocaine) by 80 minutes; saline stays near 90–100% throughout. Group means with standard errors only; n = 4 (cocaine), 7 (cocaethylene), 7 (saline).

key_findings.finding: In rats given 10 mg/kg intraperitoneally, cocaethylene and cocaine both increased locomotor activity and rearing over 15 minutes compared with saline, with no significant difference between the two drugs (n = 5 per group).
key_findings.note: Values read from the figure at 300 dpi and approximate: saline about 22 crossings and 19 rears; cocaethylene about 68 and 47; cocaine about 86 and 81. No numerical table or test statistics are printed.

key_findings.finding: In 3 rhesus monkeys trained on intravenous cocaine, cocaethylene maintained lever responding at rates similar to or slightly higher than cocaine, with the mean maximum rate-maintaining dose 0.01 mg/kg per injection for cocaethylene against 0.03 mg/kg per injection for cocaine; higher cocaethylene doses reduced responding, as the authors note happens with most self-administered drugs including cocaine.
key_findings.note: Individual monkeys varied considerably and cocaethylene was always substituted after cocaine in the same animals. The decimal points in the figure's axis labels are not legible on the printed page, so no values were read from Fig. 5.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the effects of cocaine, ethanol and cocaethylene in combination were not addressed by these experiments, and that the human implications of their rodent data rest on the monkey self-administration findings.

reporting_issues.issue: No test statistics, degrees of freedom, standard deviations or confidence intervals are printed anywhere in the paper; the statistics section names ANOVA with the Newman-Keuls test and a threshold of P < 0.05, and every comparison is then reported in words ('significant', 'no significant difference') against figures showing group means.
reporting_issues.consequence: No result can be re-checked arithmetically, no effect size can be computed, and repeated statements that cocaethylene and cocaine did not differ, in groups of 3 to 7 animals, cannot be distinguished from low power.

reporting_issues.issue: Rat strain, sex, weight and supplier are nowhere reported, and the paper carries no animal-care or ethics approval statement; monkey sex and weights are likewise absent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The animal findings cannot be placed by species characteristics known to affect stimulant responses, and SYRCLE items on baseline characteristics cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The IC50 values are printed once per assay (300 nM for binding, 250 nM for uptake) without separate figures for cocaine and cocaethylene and without the number of concentrations, so the equipotency claim rests on overlapping curves in a figure whose points are means of 2 or 3 assays.
reporting_issues.consequence: Equipotency at the dopamine transporter should be cited from this source as an overlap of concentration-response curves, not as a measured ratio with an interval.

reporting_issues.issue: In the self-administration figure the decimal points of both axes are lost in printing, so the dose axis reads as 001, 01, 1 and the response axis as 00, 05, 10, 15, 20, 25.
reporting_issues.consequence: No value can be read from this figure; the dose range and the maximum rate-maintaining doses are available only from the Methods and Results text.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary describes cocaethylene as approximately equipotent to cocaine in maintaining responding, while the Results give a mean maximum rate-maintaining dose of 0.01 mg/kg per injection for cocaethylene against 0.03 mg/kg per injection for cocaine, and the Discussion speaks of a similar dose-response curve.
reporting_issues.consequence: The three statements are not interchangeable. What the data support is that cocaethylene maintained self-administration across a comparable dose range in 3 monkeys, with its peak rate at a lower dose than cocaine's.

reporting_issues.issue: For the 7 post-mortem samples the paper does not state the specimen site, the interval between death and sampling, storage conditions, or the cause and manner of death, and it reports no analysis of specimens from deaths without cocaine.
reporting_issues.consequence: The concentrations in Table I cannot be interpreted as ante-mortem concentrations or related to any outcome; after death, drug concentrations can change with site and time. The series supports presence after combined use and nothing about cause.
